properties.name: Bunbury Road
properties.description: The road and the community were named for Bunbury Farm at the road’s eastern end. The name Bunbury was given by John Bovyer who settled there about 1798, for his ancestral home in Cheshire, England.  The road was present, though not named, on an 1849 partial survey plan of Lot 48 and the 1863 Lake Map . In the 1881 Meacham’s Atlas, the road ran from Kelly’s Cove to Fullerton’s Marsh, and is labeled as “Bunberry Road”.  The lower Bunbury Road, west of the Mason Road, dates only to the mid-20th century. The original section of Bunbury Road west of Mason Road was renamed Clifton Road.

properties.name: Cable Court

properties.name: Captain James Crescent
properties.description: Located off of Swallow Drive. The first Kelly to Bunbury was Captain James Kelly. He was a ship's captain and ship builder in the community, having built and captained The Bunbury, among others. He had a brickyard on the property. Before there was a bridge to Charlottetown, he kept scows to transport travelers across the river to Charlottetown. In 1848, he donated the land for the Methodist Chapel (now Clifton United Church).

properties.name: Dorothy Avenue
properties.description: Names after Mrs. Dorothy Lantz, who owned the subdivision land.

properties.name: Duffy Road
properties.description: Duffy Road is named after the Duffy family whose paternal ancestor Patrick Duffy came to Bunbury from Ireland in 1834.  The Duffy farm is identified on the 1863 Lake Map of PEI.  The 1880 Meacham’s Atlas shows P. Duffy possessing 90 acres. While the Duffy dwelling is shown in 1880 map, there is no road indicated.  The 1928 Atlas shows the road stretching from the Bunbury Road to the Hillsborough River between the farms of Herbert Mason and William Duffy.  With the opening of the Hillsborough Bridge in 1905, a rail line running from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour crossed the Duffy Road. The rail line was abandoned in the early 1960s.

properties.name: Flourish Heights
properties.description: The Developers of the Foxwoods subdivision decided to use this name for the following reason; "We decided to use Flourish Street as our main street name, with six assorted colour flower names for other six roads. Flourish means prosperity, which give people an image about a lot of flowers booming, so we chose six different colour flowers as our remainder roads. Also, in Chinese, 6 and 7 are a lucky number; 6 means everything goes very well and 7 means a colourful and meaningful life; thus, 6+1 names include both these two meanings. Besides, all these flowers can be easily found on the island because we hope islanders can feel the street names are close to our life".

properties.name: Hamms Lane
properties.description: Named for and owned by the Hamm family, who came to PEI from Tor Point, Cornwall, England, and settled in Bunbury, farming the land along the mouth of Fullerton’s Creek. Meacham’s 1880 Atlas shows “Mrs. M. Hamm” with 110 acres.  Charles B. Hamm and Allan Hamm from this property served in the First World War.  Several members of the Hamm family currently have houses on this lane, representing the 5th, 6th, and 7th generations.

properties.name: Hopeton Road
properties.description: Hopeton Road is named after Hopeton, the name of this general area and specifically the farm of William Mutch who owned 170 acres at this site. William Mutch was known as “Woodhouse” William to distinguish him from his uncle and neighbor “Brickhouse” William who lived in the brick house on the adjacent farm. The heritage home of Dr. George Dewar was built on this road in 1903.  At the time, the road was a continuation of the Stratford Road. Not until the TransCanada Highway was opened in 1958, severing this short stretch of road, did it require a name separate from the road across the highway.

properties.name: Mason Road
properties.description: Until at least 1865, Mason Road was the sole entry into the community of Bunbury, entering from Cross Roads to the south  (By 1880, a beach road connected the west end of Bunbury Road to Southport ). Mason Road was named for the Mason Family which began with William Mason, who emigrated from Birdforth, Yorkshire, England, in the early part of the nineteenth century. At one time, the Mason family owned land from the river to Cross Roads. A family member described how the Mason House on this road acquired its location. “William Mason built a log cabin down by the shore. George was their oldest son. And when he was going to be married, they knew that they had to build. William wanted to build where the log cabin was. George wanted to build way up further. So they kind of settled it and built where it is today, which is in a good place.”  Eight generations of Masons have lived on the farm. In the 1880 Meacham’s Atlas of PEI, the road is identified as “Clifton Road”, which was the name of the Mason Farm.

properties.name: Michael Thomas Way
properties.description: In January 2012 Stratford Council, on the recommendation of the Heritage Committee, named Michael Thomas Way to celebrate to accomplishments of the Island Mi’kmaq and long-time Stratford resident.  The Great Michael Thomas, as some Halifax newspapers at the turn of the last century called him, had an international reputation for long-distance running. He was born on Lennox Island in 1885, but set up a fishing business in Southport. Thomas first came to prominence when he won the Charlottetown Patriot 10 mile race in 1909. Thomas would go on to win the same race three years in a row, plus other races in the Maritimes.  He was inducted posthumously into the PEI Sports Hall of Fame in 1980.

properties.name: Perley Drive

properties.name: Shepard Drive
properties.description: In May 2012 Council again accepted the recommendation of the Town’s Heritage Committee and named a new street off of the Stratford Road Shepard Drive in remembrance of the unique contribution and long and often over-looked history of the Island’s Black community. David Shepard and Kesiah Wilson were two of four slaves that Loyalist Edmund Fanning brought with him to Prince Edward Island. Their son, Benjamin is responsible for the continuation of the Shepard family name on PEI. The Shepard family is unique in that the majority of the descendants of David and Kesiah (Wilson) Shepard remained on PEI, and account for more than fifty percent of the Black community of PEI today.  The Street was officially opened with a ribbon cutting ceremony on August 8, 2012.  In attendance were area politicians, residents, and members of the black community.  The town was honoured to have joining in the ribbon-cutting award-winning author Lawrence Hill, author of The Book of Negroes.

properties.name: Mason Road
properties.description: Until at least 1865, Mason Road was the sole entry into the community of Bunbury, entering from Cross Roads to the south  (By 1880, a beach road connected the west end of Bunbury Road to Southport ). Mason Road was named for the Mason Family which began with William Mason, who emigrated from Birdforth, Yorkshire, England, in the early part of the nineteenth century. At one time, the Mason family owned land from the river to Cross Roads. A family member described how the Mason House on this road acquired its location. “William Mason built a log cabin down by the shore. George was their oldest son. So they kind of settled it and built where it is today, which is in a good place.”  Eight generations of Masons have lived on the farm. In the 1880 Meacham’s Atlas of PEI, the road is identified as “Clifton Road”, which was the name of the Mason Farm.

properties.name: Michael Thomas Way
properties.description: In January 2012 Stratford Council, on the recommendation of the Heritage Committee, named Michael Thomas Way to celebrate to accomplishments of the Island Mi’kmaq and long-time Stratford resident.  The Great Michael Thomas, as some Halifax newspapers at the turn of the last century called him, had an international reputation for long-distance running. He was born on Lennox Island in 1885, but set up a fishing business in Southport. Thomas first came to prominence when he won the Charlottetown Patriot 10 mile race in 1909. Thomas would go on to win the same race three years in a row, plus other races in the Maritimes.  He was inducted posthumously into the PEI Sports Hall of Fame in 1980.

So they kind of settled it and built where it is today, which is in a good place.”  Eight generations of Masons have lived on the farm. In the 1880 Meacham’s Atlas of PEI, the road is identified as “Clifton Road”, which was the name of the Mason Farm.

properties.name: McCallum Drive
properties.description: The street is named after the McCallum family, as the 1880 Atlas shows the McCallums as the property owners of the land within this area.

properties.name: McLean Lane
properties.description: Named for the McLean family, who own much of the property in the area.

properties.name: Michael Thomas Way
properties.description: In January 2012 Stratford Council, on the recommendation of the Heritage Committee, named Michael Thomas Way to celebrate to accomplishments of the Island Mi’kmaq and long-time Stratford resident.  The Great Michael Thomas, as some Halifax newspapers at the turn of the last century called him, had an international reputation for long-distance running. He was born on Lennox Island in 1885, but set up a fishing business in Southport. Thomas first came to prominence when he won the Charlottetown Patriot 10 mile race in 1909. Thomas would go on to win the same race three years in a row, plus other races in the Maritimes.  He was inducted posthumously into the PEI Sports Hall of Fame in 1980.

properties.name: Millbrook Drive
properties.description: Named after Millbrook House - owned by the Rogersons.

properties.name: Myrtle Street
properties.description: Named after Myrtle Jenkins, wife of Hollis Jenkins the owner of the land that was sold to the Stratford Business Park.

properties.name: Orchard Drive
properties.description: The subdivision, Reeve's Estates, used to be an apple orchard.

properties.name: Perley Drive
properties.description: The street is named after W. Perley Mutch, who grew up, married, and raised his own family in the “brick house” on Stratford Road. Furthermore, the new road extends down the farm on which Perley worked his entire life, and “The Barn”, which existed on this property, was built by Perley for his Holstein cattle and later became a popular restaurant before burning in the 80’s.

properties.name: Red Rock Lane
properties.description: A well known resident, Bill Rix, lived in the area and owned a brewery which produced Red Rock Ale.

properties.name: Reddin Heights
properties.description: Named after the Reddin family who owned the land.

properties.name: Reeves Boulevard
properties.description: Named after Malcolm Reeves, owner of the land which later became Reeves Estates.

properties.name: Reta Gerry Lane
properties.description: Former Smallwood Property; they were active in harness racing in the province and had owned, trained and raced Gold Cup winning horses. The developers named the street after both of their mothers, Reta and Gerry.

properties.name: Saints Crescent
properties.description: Named after Jack Saint, owner of some of the lands in the Kinlock Creek Subdivision.

properties.name: Saul's Pride Crescent
properties.description: Former Smallwood Property; they were active in harness racing in the province and had owned, trained, and raced Gold Cup winning horses. The street is named after the Gold Cup winning horse, Saul’s Pride, which won in 1980 and 1982.

properties.name: Shakespear Drive
properties.description: Named after playwright William Shakespeare. Several streets in Stratford have been named after characters in his plays.

properties.name: Shepard Drive
properties.description: In May 2012 Council again accepted the recommendation of the Town’s Heritage Committee and named a new street off of the Stratford Road Shepard Drive in remembrance of the unique contribution and long and often over-looked history of the Island’s Black community. David Shepard and Kesiah Wilson were two of four slaves that Loyalist Edmund Fanning brought with him to Prince Edward Island. Their son, Benjamin is responsible for the continuation of the Shepard family name on PEI. The Shepard family is unique in that the majority of the descendants of David and Kesiah (Wilson) Shepard remained on PEI, and account for more than fifty percent of the Black community of PEI today.  The Street was officially opened with a ribbon cutting ceremony on August 8, 2012.  In attendance were area politicians, residents, and members of the black community.  The town was honoured to have joining in the ribbon-cutting award-winning author Lawrence Hill, author of The Book of Negroes.

properties.name: Smallwood Terrace
properties.description: The family of Henry Smallwood lived in the old house on the Mason Road. As a youngster, Joey Smallwood, first premier of Newfoundland, would spend time here visiting his Island cousins. The father of Joe and Henry Smallwood of harness racing fame was raised here.

properties.name: Squire Lane
properties.description: Named after Squire McCarron owner of lands in the area.

properties.name: St. Catherines Avenue
properties.description: Named by Bryer Jones, owner of the subdivision.

properties.name: St. John Avenue
properties.description: The street name came from a seniors rental apartment building, St. John House, owned by St. John Ambulance, which is located on the street.

properties.name: Stratford Road
properties.description: Main street in the Town and the name goes back in history to 1850 - 1860 or earlier.

properties.name: Strawberry Lane
properties.description: Named after the area which was designated in the 1880 Atlas as Strawberry Hill.

properties.name: Towerwood Drive
properties.description: The TV/Cable Tower is located adjacent to the road and is is located in the woods.

properties.name: Tulip Crescent
properties.description: The Developers of the subdivision decided to use these names for the following reason; "We decided to use Flourish Heights as our main street name, with six assorted colour flower names for other six roads. Flourish means prosperity, which give people an image about a lot of flowers blooming, so we chose six different colour flowers as our remainder roads. Also, in Chinese, 6 and 7 are a lucky number; 6 means everything goes very well and 7 means a colourful and meaningful life; thus, 6+1 names include both these two meanings. Besides, all these flowers can be easily found on the island because we hope islanders can feel the street names are close to our life..."

properties.name: Winjoe Drive
properties.description: The street name is a combination of the names of two of the Rodgerson girls.

properties.name: Woodhouse Court
properties.description: The property was owned by William Mutch, and there was also another William Mutch within Stratford who owned the Brick house on the Stratford Road, who were Uncle and Nephew to each other. To aid in distinguishing between the two William Mutch’s, the descriptions of the Brick House and the Wood House were adopted as middle names for each due to the different building materials each of their homes was made of.

properties.name: Zakem Heights
properties.description: Named after Albert Zakem, who owned & subdivided most of the land in that area.
